packageRules.description: Group all Spring Boot and Spring Framework dependencies

A patch merges itself once the required checks passed. The builds of these repositories run their own tests against a real engine or cluster, so a green pipeline is a strong statement for a patch. What that statement does not cover is listed in the rules below, which come after this one and therefore win.
Tools and test libraries merge themselves for a minor as well: they never reach a released artifact, and a break shows up as a red build rather than as behaviour in production.
The workflows of the repository are covered by the run that uses them, so a minor and a digest merge themselves too.

The Spring Boot and Quarkus versions are a promise: the README of each repository names the platform versions it is built against, and an application picks them itself. Moving one is a decision about what is supported, so it is read and merged by a person even when the build is green.

The BPMS itself is never merged by a robot. The engine or the client a build was compiled against decides which server versions the artifact accepts, which is a statement about every application that consumes it, and a green build says nothing about the clusters nobody here runs. The Camunda 8 adapter refines this per release line in its own configuration.
A major is read by a person. It is the update where a green build proves the least, since nothing compiles differently until something behaves differently.
